chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Barqi, from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan al-Dinawari, who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, what do you say regarding the Christian woman? Do I buy her and sell her from the Christians?' He said, 'Buy and sell.' I said, 'Then do I marry her?' He remained silent for a while, then looked at me and said, almost in concealment, 'She is lawful for you.'
He said. I said, 'May I be your ransom, do I buy the singer or the maid who is good at singing, intending by her the provision (livelihood) and nothing else?' He said, 'Buy and sell.'

key_terms.شِبْهَ الْإِخْفَاءِ: Almost in concealment / as if hiding

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying and selling Christian women or female singers for livelihood in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the commercial and marital permissibility of Christian women, distinguishing between general trade and the specific ruling on marriage. While the initial query about marriage elicited a brief pause before confirming their lawfulness, the Imam explicitly permits acquiring female singers or slaves for livelihood, reflecting the practical economic realities of the Shia community under Abbasid rule. This highlights the flexibility in personal status laws regarding *Kitabiyyat* (Women of the Book) within the framework of *Makasib* (earnings).
